analysis.one_liner: Lets the government negotiate Medicare drug prices directly with manufacturers and pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsor in two years and died in committee when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let the Secretary of Health and Human Services negotiate prices with drug manufacturers and pharmacies for drugs covered under Medicare Part D. It would replace the current law provision that says the government may not interfere with negotiations between drug makers and the private plans that provide the Medicare drug benefit. The bill was referred to two House committees, then to their health subcommittees, and was never considered further.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, particularly seniors and people with disabilities in the Part D drug program, if lower negotiated prices were passed through as lower drug costs and premiums. Plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage organizations would also pay less for the drugs they buy.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would allow the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate with drug manufacturers and pharmacies over the prices paid for Medicare Part D covered drugs.

It would replace the current provision of law directing the Secretary not to interfere with negotiations between drug manufacturers and pharmacies and the private Part D plans, which is the legal reason the government does not bargain for seniors today.

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers and pharmacies, which would face direct government negotiation over the prices Medicare Part D plans pay for covered drugs. The bill imposes no new taxes and no cost on beneficiaries.

drawbacks.text: The bill only 'authorizes' negotiation; it does not require the Secretary to negotiate any specific drug or give the government a fallback like a binding price or a public option, so the Secretary could choose not to negotiate at all.

The bill does not require plan sponsors or Medicare Advantage organizations to pass any savings from negotiated prices to beneficiaries, so lower negotiated input prices could be absorbed by the plans rather than reaching seniors.
The bill drew no cosponsors, including from the sponsor's own party, suggesting it was not viewed as a serious vehicle even as larger drug negotiation bills moved in the same Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real: government negotiation of Medicare drug prices is the mechanism drug-price advocates have long sought, and the bill would strike the current-law non-interference clause that blocks it. But the bill as written is a weak instrument. It merely authorizes negotiation with no requirement to act, no enforcement mechanism, and no guarantee that savings flow to beneficiaries rather than to the plans. A serious version would mandate negotiation for high-cost drugs and require savings to lower premiums and copays. As drafted, its main value was symbolic, and the record shows it never attracted the support to become anything more.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee the whole time: it was sent to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees, and neither ever acted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 4, 2007 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees.
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Health of each committee in February 2007 and received no further action.
The bill attracted no cosponsors, including none from the sponsor's own party.
Congress ended on January 3, 2009 without the bill receiving a markup, floor vote, or any consideration in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers and pharmacies are better off because the bill never advanced; the existing system, in which the government cannot interfere with price setting between drug makers and Part D plans, stayed in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers kept the existing pricing system

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan line formed.

industries.note: The bill would give the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority to negotiate prices charged to Part D plans and Medicare Advantage organizations for covered drugs, replacing the current-law 'non-interference' provision [S2] [S3]. Government negotiation is the main lever for lowering drug prices for seniors, and brand-name manufacturers have consistently fought it.
Pharmacies would be subject to negotiated prices alongside manufacturers [S2] [S3]. Their interest in negotiating depends on whether negotiated prices preserve dispensing margins.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plans and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: The bill directs negotiation over prices charged to prescription drug plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage organizations, so the plans themselves are not the negotiating party; they pay whatever is negotiated [S2]. Lower input prices could help their margins, but a government negotiator also displaces their private contracting role with drug makers.
